question.text: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the emergency room with hyperextension of the cervical spine caused by a trampoline injury. After ruling out the possibility of hemorrhagic shock, she is diagnosed with quadriplegia with neurogenic shock. The physical examination is most likely to reveal which of the following constellation of findings?

options.A: Pulse: 110/min; blood pressure: 88/50 mm Hg; respirations: 26/min; normal rectal tone on digital rectal examination (DRE); normal muscle power and sensations in the limbs
options.B: Pulse: 99/min; blood pressure: 188/90 mm Hg; respirations: 33/min; loss of rectal tone on DRE; reduced muscle power and absence of sensations in the limbs
options.C: Pulse: 56/min; blood pressure: 88/40 mm Hg; respirations: 22/min; loss of rectal tone on DRE; reduced muscle power and absence of sensations in the limbs
options.D: Pulse: 54/min; blood pressure: 88/44 mm Hg; respirations: 26/min; increased rectal tone on DRE; normal muscle power and sensations in the limbs
options.E: Pulse: 116/min; blood pressure: 80/40 mm Hg; respirations: 16/min; loss of rectal tone on DRE; reduced muscle power and absence of sensations in the limbs

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The patient presents with quadriplegia and neurogenic shock following cervical spine injury. Neurogenic shock is characterized by hypotension, bradycardia, and absent reflexes. The physical exam findings of loss of rectal tone, reduced muscle power, and absence of sensations in the limbs are consistent with this diagnosis. The other options do not align with the expected findings of neurogenic shock.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: Loss of rectal tone on DRE is a key indicator of neurogenic shock.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: Hemorrhagic shock was ruled out, so that is not a consideration. Spinal cord injury with compression could cause similar symptoms, but the presence of neurogenic shock points more strongly to the spinal cord injury itself causing the shock.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient has quadriplegia with neurogenic shock, indicating spinal cord injury at or above C5. Neurogenic shock causes hypotension, bradycardia, and tachypnea. Loss of rectal tone and reduced muscle power/sensations in limbs are consistent with spinal cord injury. Option C shows bradycardia (56/min), hypotension (88/40 mm Hg), and tachypnea (22/min) with neurological deficits, matching the diagnosis.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: Bradycardia (56/min) and hypotension (88/40 mm Hg) with neurological deficits
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Hemorrhagic shock was ruled out, so spinal cord injury is the primary diagnosis. Other causes of shock (e.g., cardiogenic, obstructive) were less likely given the neurological findings.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient has quadriplegia with neurogenic shock, which typically presents with bradycardia (low pulse), hypotension (low BP), and loss of autonomic function including loss of rectal tone. Reduced muscle power and absent sensation in limbs are expected with quadriplegia. Option C matches all these findings: bradycardia (56/min), hypotension (88/40 mm Hg), loss of rectal tone, and neurologic deficits.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: Loss of rectal tone on DRE and reduced muscle power with absent sensation are hallmark signs of spinal cord injury at cervical level causing neurogenic shock and quadriplegia.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Hemorrhagic shock was ruled out, so neurogenic shock is the correct diagnosis. Other options show tachycardia or hypertension inconsistent with neurogenic shock, or normal neurologic findings inconsistent with quadriplegia.

olmo3_7b.clinical_reasoning: The patient has cervical spine hyperextension injury with quadriplegia and neurogenic shock, indicating high spinal cord involvement above the C1 level. Neurogenic shock presents with hypotension (systolic 88 mm Hg), tachycardia (pulse 56/min), and tachypnea (respirations 22/min). Loss of lower limb motor tone and sensation is expected, while increased rectal tone (C) suggests autonomic dysreflexia or spasticity, which is atypical in this context. Options A, B, D, and E do not appropriately reflect the expected findings of spinal cord injury at or above the cervical level.
olmo3_7b.critical_evidence: Hypotension and tachycardia consistent with neurogenic shock due to spinal cord injury above the cervical spine.
olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Other options either show normal or inappropriate vital signs (A, B, D) or contradictory findings regarding motor tone (E). Only C's hypotension aligns with the severity of cervical spine injury and neurogenic shock.
